content: A ganglion cyst, also referred to as a Bible bump, is a swelling that typically develops on or around joints and tendons, most commonly in the hand or foot. The size of the cyst can fluctuate over time and may become more inflamed if irritated. These cysts are most frequently found around the wrist and on the fingers. The exact cause of ganglion cyst formation remains unknown. However, it is believed that repetitive overuse of a specific joint may lead to degeneration of the surrounding fibrous tissue, resulting in the development of a cystic structure. The cyst is filled with a clear fluid that resembles synovial fluid. Approximately 90% of ganglion cysts occur around the wrist joint. A common misconception is that these cysts are caused by protruding pockets of synovium from the joint capsule, but this does not explain the toughness of the cyst wall. Diagnosis of a ganglion cyst typically involves a physical examination. The appearance of the cyst can be observed and is often adapted from dermatological references. In many cases, ganglion cysts resolve on their own over time. For small cysts that do not cause symptoms, no treatment is necessary. If the cyst is symptomatic, it can be treated through aspiration or surgical excision. Aspiration is a simpler procedure but has a recurrence rate of approximately 50%. Surgical excision reduces the recurrence rate to 5–10%, and complications are rare. Immobilizing the hand or finger for 1–2 weeks after treatment can further lower the recurrence rate. Arthroscopy of the wrist is emerging as a viable alternative to open excision. This minimally invasive procedure allows direct visualization of the cyst's origin, and no immobilization is required post-procedure. Historically, a traditional method of treating ganglion cysts involved striking the lump with a heavy book, such as a Bible, to rupture the cyst and allow its contents to drain into the surrounding tissues. This practice gave rise to the nickname Bible bumps or Gideon’s disease. While this method was effective, it is no longer recommended due to the risk of causing damage to the surrounding tissues. Ganglion cysts are most commonly observed in individuals aged 20–60 years and are three times more prevalent in women than in men.
